question.knowledge_point: Solving an Inequality Involving Two Logarithmic Functions
question.worked_solution:
We use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $e.$ This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+2)-5} & \ge {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)} \\ {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+2)}\cdot {e}^{-5} & \ge {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)} \\ (x+2){e}^{-5} & \ge 3x \\ x+2 & \ge 3{e}^{5}x \\ 2 & \ge (3{e}^{5}-1)x \\ \frac{2}{3{e}^{5}-1} & \ge x\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithms in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithms, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2 & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & >-2 \\ 3x & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & >0\end{aligned}
$$

Our solution is $x\le \frac{2}{3{e}^{5}-1},$ which can be expressed as $(-\infty ,\frac{2}{3{e}^{5}-1}].$ Additionally, the domains of the logarithms are $x>-2$ and $x>0,$ which can be expressed as $(-2,\infty )$ and $(0,\infty )$ respectively. To find the solutions that are in the domains of the logarithms, we take the intersection:

$$
(-\infty ,\frac{2}{3{e}^{5}-1}]\cap (-2,\infty )\cap (0,\infty )=(0,\frac{2}{3{e}^{5}-1}]
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in (0,\frac{2}{3{e}^{5}-1}],$ which can also be written as $0<x\le \frac{2}{3{e}^{5}-1}.$
